metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
In data center retrofits, the structural floor can bind before the electrical supply does, because liquid-cooled AI racks weigh far more than the enterprise racks buildings were engineered for.

The weight comes from what the rack now contains: coolant, manifolds, and batteries. Those are additions to the rack itself, not to the building, so the load arrives with the hardware while the slab or raised floor stays as originally poured. The metric is the structural weight supported per square foot against the actual weight of installed racks, which makes it a comparison between a fixed building and a moving target.

That matters for AI because rack density is the direction of travel. Every increment of compute packed into a cabinet adds mass that the floor must carry, so floor loading becomes a siting question rather than a detail settled late in a project. It sits in the same category as server utilization and stranded power and space per cabinet, which are the other measures of how much capacity a given facility can actually absorb.

What the data does not give is magnitude. There are no load limits, no rack weights, no count of affected sites, and no cost or schedule figures. The claim that retrofits hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than expected is stated as an industry observation, not quantified here, and nothing in the data distinguishes new construction from retrofit or one region from another.
